claims.claim: Practice data prompt specifies $3,420 total discrepancy but NOT the breakdown
claims.evidence: The report quotes the practice data prompt as specifying '$892,000 deposits, $876,580 withdrawals, $3,420 discrepancy' and notes it specifies 'timing differences, a bank charge not yet posted to the GL, and one unidentified item' (categories) but not specific counts, dollar amounts per category, or descriptions. The borderline judgment note confirms the categories are seeded but the decomposition is fabricated.

claims.claim: Commands (not skills) are the correct invocation pattern for Ch17
claims.evidence: The report explains that Exercises 5-7 use /command-name format for Cowork plugin commands and that this is correct for Ch17. This is consistent with the plugin architecture where commands are the user-facing invocation method.

suggestions.assertion: Identifies inline data injection or paste-based patterns in exercise prompts
suggestions.reason: This assertion is somewhat ambiguous — it could mean D3 (inline data injection into prompts) or the broader pattern of fabricated data embedded in lesson content. The skill found D1 (fabricated output) rather than D3, which is arguably a different defect class. The assertion would be more discriminating if it specified: 'Identifies fabricated agent output embedded in lesson narrative (D1 defects)' vs 'Identifies raw data pasted into prompts instead of file references (D3 defects)'. As written, a skill that found only D3 issues OR only D1 issues would pass, but these are different quality problems.

No assertion checks whether the recommended fixes preserve the pedagogical intent of the original content. The audit report's suggested replacements (intent tables, generalised narrative) are high quality, but an audit that simply deleted the fabricated content without replacement would also pass all 5 assertions. Consider adding: 'Recommended fixes include replacement content that preserves the teaching objective (not just deletion).'

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions are well-targeted for this eval case. The Ch17/Ch18+ terminology distinction (expectations 1 and 5) is the strongest discriminator — it tests domain-specific judgment that a generic audit would fail. The main gap is that no assertion verifies the quality of recommended fixes.
